activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Mason stood at the school store counter, holding the last five dollars of his allowance. The new Calder sports drink, the one in the bright green bottle, cost exactly five dollars, and the line behind him stretched all the way to the gym doors. Callan nudged him from behind. "Everyone's buying it," Callan said. "The whole basketball team drinks it. Lionel got two."

Everyone. That word had a pull to it, like a tide. Mason set his money on the counter, then picked it up again. "Hold on," he said, and stepped aside to check his phone one last time.

The night before, he had watched a video review of the drink over and over. A famous sprinter he followed held up the green bottle and called it "revolutionary, unstoppable, a game-changer," words that seemed to sparkle when he said them. Mason had almost asked his mom to order a case right then. The only thing that stopped him was a small detail he'd noticed at the edge of the screen, a little hashtag tucked into the caption: #ad.

He scrolled back to the video now, in the hallway by the water fountain. There it was again, tiny as a crumb. He remembered what Ms. Luo had mentioned during their media unit, almost in passing, that in the United States the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something. Mason had written it in his notebook because it seemed like a hidden rule, a way to see something invisible. The sprinter hadn't been raving about the drink because he loved it. He'd been paid, and the hashtag was the label on that fact.

Mason tried a small test. He looked up three more reviews of the drink. Two ordinary kids gave it lukewarm ratings, saying it tasted like flat lime soda. The only glowing one was from a celebrity, and it ended with #ad. A pattern, plain as the tiles on the hallway floor. The loaded words started to sound less like magic and more like a script. Callan's "everyone's buying it" started to sound like propaganda, the kind that makes you want to join a crowd before you check where the crowd is going.

"You getting it or not?" the cashier asked. Mason looked at the green bottle, then at the plain water fountain two steps away, free and cold.

"Not getting it," Mason said, and pocketed his five dollars. "But if you want something unstoppable, try that fountain."

Callan laughed, and the line moved on without them.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
John had practiced the piano piece nine times, but the church basement where the youth band rehearsed was not his living room, and the old upright piano against the wall knew it. The band was getting ready to play for the Saturday service, and Mr. Zhou, who ran the band and also played bass, had spread the sheet music across the music stands with a look that said the tempo markings mattered.

Halfway through the second run-through, the song fell apart. Malakai's drums slowed down at the spot marked rit., but Edgar's guitar kept charging ahead like a dog that had spotted a squirrel, and the whole thing crashed into a pile of noise. Edgar lowered his guitar. "Malakai, why'd you hit the brakes?"

"Because it says rit.," Malakai said, pointing at the page. "Ritardando means gradually slowing down."

"Then why didn't everyone else?"

That was the question, John realized. He leaned over Edgar's music stand and studied the marking. If rit. meant everyone slowed down gradually, then the strange word later in the piece, accelerando, probably meant the opposite, gradually speeding up, and it made sense that half the band had missed it because the print was tiny. But guessing was not the same as knowing. "Let's test it," John said. "Mr. Zhou, can Malakai and I play just those eight bars, no guitar, no voices?"

Mr. Zhou nodded and counted them in.

Malakai slowed into the rit. exactly as written, and John followed him on the piano, letting each note stretch a little longer than the one before it. It sounded like a song exhaling. Then they hit the accelerando and pushed forward together, quicker with every measure, and it sounded like the song had woken up.

"Okay, I hear it now," Edgar said, though his guitar had gone mysteriously quiet and one string appeared to need urgent tuning. "It's not arbitrary, what the composer wrote. There's a reason."

"There is," Mr. Zhou said. "Now all of you, together. And Edgar, no retiring from this part, no matter how much your string complains."

They ran it four more times. The first was rough, the second was better, and by the fourth, the whole band slowed and sped up as one body, and even Edgar's stubborn string behaved. John felt the piano keys under his fingers respond to Malakai's drums instead of fighting them, like the two of them were breathing the same air.

Afterward Malakai flopped onto a folding chair. "When the protagonist of this story becomes famous, I'm taking credit for the rit."

"Deal," John said, and played the slowing bars one more time, just to hear them breathe.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
Anthony had noticed something strange about his soccer season: the harder Cameron practiced, the slower he got. Cameron showed up at Riverside Park every single day, even Sundays, running drills until his shirt stuck to his back. Anthony came four days a week, and lately he was the one winning their one-on-one races.

"It doesn't make sense," Cameron said, breathing hard after losing again. "I do way more than you."

Anthony wanted to win, sure, but he wanted his friend sharp for Saturday's game against the Northside team. That night he lay on his bed turning the problem over. His assumption had always been that practice made you better in a straight line, more hours, more speed. But the evidence at the park said otherwise. Maybe something invisible was going on, something that happened between the workouts rather than during them.

The next morning he found Mr. Fraser, the retired gym teacher who walked his dog by the fields every day, and asked him straight out. Mr. Fraser laughed. "Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself," he said, tossing the dog its ball. "Rest days are part of getting better. Ask any coach." Then he walked on, and Anthony stood there with the whole answer rearranging itself in his head.

He decided to test it, because a theory was only a theory. He told Cameron his plan: five days on, two full days off, no sneaking to the park on the rest days. Cameron looked doubtful but agreed, since his old plan was clearly diminishing his speed. They told Braylon too, and Braylon made a chart, marking every rest day with a big blue star so it felt like an accomplishment instead of a cheat.

Saturday arrived, bright and cold. In the first half Cameron hung back, guarding his legs like they might betray him. But in the second half, with the score tied, he chased down a long ball that nobody thought he could reach, cut inside, and smashed it past the keeper. The Northside parents groaned; Braylon screamed so loudly that a jogger stopped to stare.

After the game the boys flopped onto the grass near the fountain, still in their muddy cleats. "So rest days are part of getting better," Cameron said slowly, like he was tasting the words. "Official part. With stars and everything." Anthony bumped his fist. "Blue ones," he said.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The noon Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer than in winter, so shadows at noon are shorter in summer.
story:
Megan stood barefoot in the backyard with a ruler, a notebook, and a problem. On Monday she had to explain to her class why Earth's tilt causes the seasons, and Lydia had already announced that Lydia knew the real answer. "It's because we're closer to the Sun in summer," Lydia had said at lunch, and Harper had nodded along. Megan needed proof that Lydia was wrong, and she only had the weekend.

The fence post near the garden was her best clue. Her dad had scribbled its noon shadow length on the shed wall last December, when he was figuring out where to put a planter: "Dec. 20, noon, 96 cm." Ninety-six centimeters was nearly as long as Megan's whole leg. Today, in late June, the sun felt like it was pressing down on her shoulders, and she wondered what the shadow would say about it now.

At exactly noon, she crouched beside the post and measured. Nine centimeters. She measured again, pressing the ruler flat against the ground. Nine. She wrote it down, then stared at the two numbers like they were a message in code. What could make the same post throw a long shadow in winter and a short one now? She imagined the Sun sliding up and down the sky like a marble on a string, and wondered if the string had different lengths at different times of year. A shadow gets shorter, she thought, only when the light comes from higher up. So the noon Sun must climb higher in summer than it does in winter. That was it. That was the whole secret hiding in the shed-wall scribble.

She ran inside to sketch it. On paper she drew the post twice, once with a long slanted shadow, once with a stubby one, and an arrow labeled "Sun higher" over the summer picture. If the Sun itself were higher and lower, then distance alone couldn't be the answer. Lydia's idea started to wobble in Megan's mind. The tilt, then. Earth leaned, and somehow that leaning changed how high the noon Sun climbed, which changed the shadows, which changed everything else. How the lean did that, Megan couldn't yet see; it was like a frontier she was standing at, able to see the far edge but not cross. She flipped to a fresh page and started a list of questions.

Harper came over that afternoon to swim, and Megan dragged her to the fence first. "Measure it yourself," she said, holding out the ruler. Harper knelt down, squinting at the tiny dark line beside the post. "Nine centimeters," Harper reported. "And in December it was ninety-six." Harper looked up at the blazing white sky, then at Megan. "Okay," she said slowly. "I nominate you to be the one who tells Lydia she's wrong on Monday." Megan grinned and pulled her chalk from her pocket, and on the shed wall, right under her dad's note, she wrote in big molten-orange letters: "June 22, noon, 9 cm."

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: In a "pick and pop," the screener steps away from the basket to an open spot for a jump shot instead of rolling toward the hoop.
story:
Hailey stood at the top of the key with the ball and tried to remember everything Mr. Munro had written on the whiteboard. Three practices into her new job as point guard, and she still felt like the court was a chessboard where she could only see half the pieces. The other half was the defense, and the defense kept winning.

"Call something!" Claudia shouted from the wing. She was setting the screen, and every time she rolled to the hoop, the girl guarding Hailey slid through and the girl guarding Claudia switched, and the pass got swallowed up. Three times in a row. The bleachers were almost empty on a Thursday evening, just a few parents and one lonely water bottle rolling along the baseline, but Hailey still felt like everyone could see her failing.

She thought about it while she dribbled. The defense expected the roll. They were watching for Claudia to cut toward the basket, because that was what had happened every time. So what if Claudia did the opposite? There was a word for it, something Mr. Munro had mentioned once, a variation on the play. Hailey couldn't remember the whole explanation, only the shape of it: the screener goes away from the basket instead of toward it.

"Pick and pop!" Hailey called, loud enough that Sophia at the corner could hear it too. Claudia set the screen on Hailey's defender, then instead of rolling to the hoop she stepped back, away from the basket, to the open spot near the free throw line. The switching defender ran the wrong way for half a second, and Claudia was alone.

Hailey fired the pass. Claudia caught it, set her feet, and shot. The ball went in, and the net made its clean little sound.

"Where did that come from?" Claudia asked, jogging back on defense.

"I figured the roll wasn't working because they kept switching," Hailey said. "So we had to give them something they weren't ready for." The empty bleachers and the scuffed floor had felt desolate an hour ago, but now the court seemed full of possibilities. She raised her voice for the next possession. "Same play. Let's see if they can stop it twice."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip has no GPS and cannot track where an animal is; it only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close.
story:
Victor carried the cardboard carrier through Riverside Park with both hands, the way Ms. Das had shown him. Inside sat a small black kitten with one white toe, which the shelter had named Rocket and which Victor was allowed to rename once he got home. The plan was simple: walk home before dark, set up the litter box, feed him, done. Then a dog off its leash came barreling across the grass, a woman shouted, and the carrier's latch popped open. Rocket shot out like a flicked marble and vanished under the line of hedges beside the tennis courts.

Victor stood there for a second, then remembered something the shelter volunteer had said. "He's microchipped," she had told him. He pulled out his phone and opened the shelter's website, looking for a map, a little dot, anything that would show him where Rocket was. Kathleen found him like that, turning his phone around as if the screen were the problem.

"Wait," she said. "My aunt works at the animal shelter. The chip has no GPS. It can't track where an animal is." She held up her hand before he could argue. "It only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close to it. Like at a checkout, scanning a price tag."

"So it's a name tag, not a tracker," Victor said slowly. That changed everything. If Rocket ran three streets away, the chip would tell a shelter whose cat he was, but it would never bring him back tonight. Nobody was coming to help him. It was just Victor, the hedges, and a kitten that could squeeze through a gap the size of a fist.

He refused to resign himself to sitting around until morning, though Lance, who biked over when Kathleen texted him, thought that was the smart move. "Cats are nocturnal," Lance said. "He'll come out when it gets dark and quiet." That was probably true, Victor thought, but Rocket was nine weeks old and had never been outside. A kitten that small wouldn't know how to find food out here, and the park emptied at dusk.

So he tested an idea. Rocket had spent the ride crying whenever the carrier stopped moving. Maybe the kitten felt safest with familiar things nearby. Victor set the open carrier on the grass by the hedges, put the soft blanket from the bottom of it beside the entrance, and crinkled the bag of kitten food Kathleen had carried from his house. Then they all backed away to the bench and sat as still as statues.

The sky turned orange, then gray. A jogger passed. Somewhere a sprinkler hissed on. Victor was starting to think Lance had been right after all when a black shape crept out from under the hedge, nose twitching, one white toe gleaming in the lamplight. Rocket sniffed the blanket, stepped inside the carrier, and curled up on it.

Victor walked over slowly and clicked the latch shut. "Good thing your chip isn't the only thing that knows you," he whispered through the air holes.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, so voices can sound muffled even when they are loud enough.
story:
Piper stood in the guest bedroom holding two pillowcases and listening to her grandmother ask "What?" for the fourth time in ten minutes. Grandma had arrived on Monday with two suitcases and a tin of lemon cookies, and she was wonderful, mostly, except that every time Piper spoke, Grandma smiled and nodded like she was guessing.

The pattern was strange. Piper's dad could shout from the kitchen and Grandma would answer instantly. Tea's knock on the front door, sharp and squeaky, got Grandma moving every time. But Piper's own voice seemed to vanish somewhere in the air between them. Last night Piper had whispered an experiment at the dinner table, low and rumbly: "There's ice cream in the freezer." Grandma had heard that fine. Then Piper had said, in her normal voice, "It's the mint kind," and Grandma had squinted and asked if Piper had mentioned the weather.

Piper dropped the pillowcases on the guest bed and grabbed her notebook, the one she used for what Harry called her "detective data." She made two columns: Heard and Didn't. High-pitched things, like the kettle's whistle and Piper's own voice, kept landing in Didn't. Low-pitched things, like Dad's voice and the rumble of the laundry downstairs, landed in Heard. It wasn't random. It was a rule, and rules could be tested. Piper remembered the summer Grandma had missed every fire alarm drill at their old apartment, how she'd complained afterward that the sirens sounded "far away and foggy." Piper had thought Grandma was being dramatic. Now she wrote Foggy at the top of her page and underlined it.

On Thursday, Piper carried her phone into the guest bedroom, where Grandma was folding a sweater into the drawer like it was origami. "Grandma, I have a theory. My voice is high, like a whistle, and I think high sounds reach you all foggy, even when I'm loud enough. Low sounds come through clear." She dropped her voice an octave. "Can you hear me now?"

"Loud and clear," Grandma said, sounding surprised. "You sound like a radio announcer."

Piper grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. "So it's not that you're ignoring me. I've been talking in the wrong pitch this whole week."

All Friday and Saturday, Piper practiced her "announcer voice," as Tea named it when Piper demonstrated at school, and by Sunday it was almost automatic. They sat together on the guest bed, the notebook between them, and Grandma pointed at the two columns. "You summarize your data better than your grandfather did, and he was an engineer." She held up one finger. "One condition. When my ears and a fancy doctor fix it, you go back to being squeaky."

"Deal," Piper said, and dropped her voice. "Now, about that tin of cookies you hid behind the sweaters."

Grandma laughed and pulled it out of the drawer.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
Payton pushed her pasta around the plate while Mael, who had stayed for dinner, told her mother about the science unit. "Mr. Berg says we have to extract the flavor oils from a lemon peel for our project," Mael said. "That's the hardest component of the whole lab, getting the oil out without squeezing the pulp in."

Payton barely heard him. She had slept badly again, third night in a row, and this morning her stomach had hurt before the spelling quiz even started. Her mother noticed her fork going nowhere.

"Payton. You've been dragging for weeks. Are you sick, or is something else going on?" Her mother's voice was gentle, but Payton hated that question because she did not know the answer. She had a theory, though. At her last checkup, the doctor had said something she kept turning over. Nikita, who had been out sick for a month with worry over her dad's surgery, had been at the same appointment day, and afterward Nikita had repeated it in the waiting room, slow, like she was memorizing it. "Cortisol," Nikita had said. "It's a hormone made by the adrenal glands, and it rises during stress. The doctor said when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high. That's why I've felt so run down."

Payton had been thinking about that ever since. Her stress had lasted a long time. The move, the new school, the math placement test she had not studied for because she could not make herself open the book. If her cortisol was staying high like Nikita's had, then being exhausted and achy made sense, and it meant the problem was not the flu. It meant the anxiety itself was the hidden cause, sitting underneath everything like a floor under a rug. She could not see it, but she could test it. Her idea was simple: if stress kept her cortisol high, then lowering the stress should lower everything that came with it.

"I think it's worry, not a cold," Payton said. "And I have a plan." She told them the plan in pieces. First, she would tell Mr. Berg tomorrow that the placement test was eating her, because saying things out loud was a kind of coping Nikita's counselor had recommended. Second, she would set a boundary around bedtime, no phone after nine, because scrolling at midnight while imagining failing the test was probably the most vulnerable moment of her whole day, the moment the worry crept in and stayed.

Mael stabbed a meatball. "You're going to tell Mr. Berg you're nervous? Out loud? To his face?"

"To his face," Payton said. She took her first real bite of pasta, and it tasted like something again. "Nine o'clock, phone in the kitchen drawer, me in bed. And tomorrow I talk to him before first bell." She pointed her fork at Mael. "You're coming with me, and you're carrying the lemon."

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are considered among the safest investments in the world.
story:
Jessica stared at the study guide Ms. Friedman had handed out on Monday. By Friday's quiz, every member of the Economics Club had to answer one question in front of the whole group, and hers had been circled in red: compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why.

"I got the easy one," said Tatiana, sliding into the seat beside her. "I just have to explain what a savings account is. Yours sounds like a trap."

"It is a trap," Jessica said. "I know a stock means you own a tiny piece of a company. If the company does well, you win. If it flops, you lose everything. A bond is more like lending your money." She flipped the paper over. "But which is riskier, and why? Ms. Friedman wants a real reason, not a guess."

Khalil leaned across the aisle. "My grandpa says stocks go up and down like a yo-yo. That's my whole answer. Up, down, yo-yo."

"That's not a reason," Tatiana said.

Khalil shrugged. "It's Friday in two days. Reasons take time."

That afternoon Jessica called her grandmother, who kept a jar of peppermints by the phone and walked with a cane now, slower and more frail than she used to be. Jessica asked her straight out, because Grandmother followed the stock market the way other grandmothers followed weather.

"Stocks or bonds, which would you pick?" Grandmother said. "For my emergency savings, never stocks. I keep every dollar of it in Treasury bonds. They're backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. People consider them among the safest investments in the world."

"Wait, backed by what?"

"The full faith and credit of the U.S. government," Grandmother repeated. "Write it down, sweetheart."

Jessica wrote it down. Then she tested it. If a bond is a loan, she thought, then the risk depends on whether the borrower can pay you back. A company can go out of business. But her grandmother's bonds weren't loans to a company. That was the hidden part, the thing you couldn't see just from the words "stock" and "bond." The risk was hiding inside who owed you the money.

On Friday, Jessica stood up when Ms. Friedman called her name. Behind her, Khalil whispered, "Yo-yo," and Tatiana patted the back of her chair as if to say, you retrieved this, now use it.

"A stock is owning a piece of a company, so it's only as safe as that company," Jessica said. "A bond is a loan. My grandmother keeps her emergency savings in Treasury bonds, and those are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. They're considered among the safest investments in the world. So a stock is riskier, because nobody guarantees a company the way the government stands behind those bonds."

Ms. Friedman drew a slow circle in the air with her marker. "And the point on the globe goes to Jessica."

"The equator," said Khalil. "It goes to the equator."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The card had arrived in Friday's homeroom pile, and Michael read it three times before he decided someone had made a mistake. It was addressed to Riley, folded inside a lumpy envelope with real stamps, and it ended with a signature that read "Fodor Bence." The problem was that Riley's grandfather was named Bence Fodor. Michael knew that from the family tree poster Riley had made for Heritage Week, which was currently taped to the gym wall next to the bake sale table.

"Your grandpa signed his own name backwards," Michael said, holding out the card as Riley dumped his backpack on the cafeteria table.

Riley took it and squinted. "He doesn't make mistakes. He's the guy who beat my dad at chess eleven times in a row."

"Then somebody at the post office mixed it up. Or you wrote the poster wrong."

"You think I invented my own grandfather?" Riley said. Julian, across the table, laughed so hard he had to put down his juice.

Michael looked at the card again. At the top, the greeting was written to "Fodor Riley," which meant Riley's whole name had been flipped, not just the grandfather's. That felt less like a mistake and more like a rule, though Michael couldn't see the rule yet. He decided to test it. He took out his phone and pulled up the class list from the school website, then went looking for kids he knew had Hungarian, Chinese, Japanese or Korean families.

Julian leaned over his shoulder. "What are you doing, detective work?"

"Sort of." The school had printed name tags for Heritage Week, and a box of the extras was still sitting in the gym. Michael found one from the Kwan family, and the tag read "Chen Kwan" even though everyone called her Kwan Chen. He found another, an anonymous entry from the art contest with no class written on it, signed "Sato Ren." The pattern was starting to compress itself in his head: every family name he could check from those places came first, and every Hungarian one did too.

He tried his logic out loud. "It's not backwards to them. It's backwards to us. Family name first, then given name, the same order they use in Chinese and Japanese and Korean."

Julian pointed a fry at him. "So when the coach calls roll and says 'Kwan, Chen,' he's accidentally speaking Chinese?"

"He's speaking gym," said Riley, but he was grinning now. He texted his dad, and the reply came back before lunch ended: "That's how Grandpa writes it. Always has. Hungarian does the same thing." Riley read it out, then looked at the card like it was a trophy.

Mr. Swampy, who had been collecting the bake sale money at the next table, glanced over. "Kovács," he said, tapping his own name tag. "Mine's the same. Try saying it backwards sometime, it's worse."

Michael copied the grandfather's signature onto his notebook and added a note underneath: same order, four languages, at least. On Monday he planned to check the school directory for every kid whose family came from somewhere he hadn't thought of yet, starting with the boy in his math class who everyone just called by his first name.

"What if we sign the group project like that?" Julian said. "Anderson Julian. Marsh Michael. It sounds like a law firm."

"It sounds like trouble," said Mr. Swampy, and slid the money box under his arm.

"Marsh Michael," Julian said again, quieter, testing it, and Michael laughed and threw his napkin at him.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
The gym had been split in half for indoor soccer practice, and Mr. Marino had set up a penalty drill at the far end. Jessica stood in line behind Charles, who kept bouncing on his toes like the floor was hot. Two spots ahead of him, Lucia gripped the ball so tightly her knuckles went pale, and Jessica could hear her breathing from three people away, quick and shallow, like a rabbit.

Jessica had been wondering about Lucia all week. She had skipped lunch twice, and yesterday she had vanished during study hall and come back with red eyes. When Jessica asked, Lucia had only said, "It's fine," in a voice that did not convey fine at all. It conveyed the opposite. There had been a brief truce between them since the fight in September, and Jessica did not want to break it by pushing. But watching Lucia now, she noticed something nobody else seemed to see. When Lucia stepped up to take her shot, she closed her eyes and let out one long, slow breath, so slow Jessica could count to five before it ended. Then she buried the ball in the corner, clean and low.

Lucia took her place in the goal for the next round, and it happened again. Charles lined up his kick, and Jessica watched Lucia's shoulders, watched her lips part, watched a breath go out slowly, longer than it came in. She looked almost calm, the opposite of the girl gripping the ball in line. Jessica turned it over in her head. It was not luck, because luck did not come in a pattern. It was something Lucia was doing on purpose, some trick she had learned. Jessica decided to test it before her own turn came, in the few seconds she had.

The line moved fast. Suddenly Charles had scored, and the ball was on the spot, and it was Jessica's kick, the one Mr. Marino would use to pick the starting lineup for Saturday. Her heart hammered and her hands felt cold, the way they did before a test, that same shaky stress that made her rush everything. She closed her eyes. In for three, out for five, long and slow, the way Lucia had done. By the end of the breath her heart had slowed just enough to feel it.

She rolled the ball into the top corner, and Lucia, back in goal, actually smiled. Walking off, Jessica caught up with her. "Where'd you learn that breathing thing?" Lucia glanced toward the hallway, toward the counselor's door with its poster about coping and anxiety, and lowered her voice. "You noticed that? I go see Ms. Reyes on Thursdays. That's where I've been." She nudged Jessica's shoulder. "Saturday, you take the first kick."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution, with a pH of about 8 to 9.
story:
The science museum's chemistry hall smelled like vinegar and old carpet, and Lea loved it anyway. She stood at the testing station with two friends, Yuvraj and Edith, staring at a tray of mystery liquids. Each liquid had a number card beside it, and the goal was to match every liquid to its pH using strips of litmus paper. The station was technically a game, but Ms. Le, who had driven them here, kept calling it "a worthy adversary," which made it sound like the tray might fight back.

Lea dipped a strip into cup A. Plain water. The paper stayed neutral, neither pink nor blue, which meant cup A was a seven. Easy. Cup B turned the strip bright pink, so it was an acid, probably the vinegar. She wrote both answers on her card and felt quietly proud, like the tray was losing.

Then came cup C, a cloudy white liquid with a faint smell of something from a kitchen cupboard. Lea dipped the strip and waited. The paper turned blue. Not bright blue, but blue.

"That's wrong," Yuvraj said, leaning over her card. "You wrote seven for this one. It has to be water with stuff in it, right? Look, the powder's even settling on the bottom."

"It's baking soda water," Edith said, squinting at the label. "Baking soda and water. Water's a seven, so this should be a seven too. It's basically water with a pinch of powder in it."

Lea looked at the blue strip again. The paper was not confused. She tapped it against the tray's edge, but it stayed blue, stubborn as a stain. Maybe the paper was broken. She pulled a fresh strip, dipped it in cup A to check, and watched it stay neutral. So the paper worked fine in plain water. That meant the baking soda was doing something she couldn't see, something the water alone didn't do. The powder looked harmless sitting there, but it had changed the liquid anyway.

"Okay," she said slowly, "so plain water is neutral, and this isn't plain water anymore. It turned blue like the soap cup did, but lighter. The soap was up around ten." She checked the color chart mounted above the tray, holding her strip next to it like she was matching a paint sample. Lighter blue than the soap, but definitely blue. "I'm saying eight. Maybe nine. Baking soda water is a mildly basic solution, pH about eight to nine."

Edith copied her answer, then paused. "My dad puts baking soda on bee stings. If it fights acid stings, maybe that's why it's not a seven. Like it's a weak base instead of a mean one."

"That's actually a good theory," Yuvraj admitted. "Don't elaborate, though. We'll be here until closing."

Ms. Le wandered over, checked their card, and raised her eyebrows at cup C. "Three for three on that tray. Would you like to try the bonus round? Five more liquids, and the clues are cumulative, so each one helps with the next."

Lea looked at the blue strip, then at the tray of new cups waiting like a dare. She picked up a fresh strip and held it over the first mystery liquid. "Watch out," she told the tray. "I've got your number now. Well. All your numbers."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them.
story:
Owen stared at the photocopied page on his desk until the letters seemed to wobble. Mr. Foster had assigned each pair of students a speech from Romeo and Juliet to transform into modern English, and Owen had drawn Juliet's speech from the balcony scene. Zaiden, his partner, leaned over and whispered, "It's like she's talking to the night sky. That's weird."

"Maybe she's just dramatic," Owen said, but something bothered him. Juliet kept saying things she would never say if Romeo were listening. She talked about how much she loved him, how she would deny her family for him, how embarrassed she was that he had overheard her. Owen read the speech a third time, then flipped back two pages. Romeo was hiding in the orchard below. Juliet was alone on her balcony, speaking her private thoughts out loud.

The next day, Mr. Foster called pairs to the front. Ronan went first with the Prince's speech, and Owen noticed that the Prince spoke to a whole crowd, declaring publicly that anyone who disturbed the peace would pay. That was different. Juliet had been talking to nobody, spilling secrets into the dark, and the audience got to hear them because she said them aloud.

"Owen and Zaiden," said Mr. Foster. Owen's palms went damp. He stood up, script in hand, and slowed himself down. When he reached the part where Juliet wondered aloud whether she was too forward, he stopped and pointed at the page.

"Here's the thing," he said. "She's alone on the balcony, and she's saying her private thoughts out loud so the audience can hear them. That's the trick. Romeo is hiding below, and she doesn't know it, so she's basically telling the whole theater a secret." He looked at Mr. Foster, half expecting to be wrong.

Mr. Foster only asked, "And what is that kind of speech called?"

"Zaiden found it," Owen said quickly.

"A soliloquy," said Zaiden, grinning.

"Correct." Mr. Foster tapped the board. "Now give me the modern version."

Owen took a breath. He imagined a girl leaning over a railing at night, the smell of cut grass drifting up from the yard, her voice low. "Okay. It sounds like this. 'Why did he have to be a Montague? It's just a name. If we called a rose something else, it would smell the same. Names aren't the problem, the fighting is. It's not like Romeo owns his name; he could drop it and keep everything that matters.' And then she realizes she's been too honest and hopes he didn't hear, except he did." Owen paused. "So the whole audience is on her side because we know something she doesn't. We're like impartial judges, and the Montague-and-Capulet feud is bad for commerce in the city too, which the Prince already said."

Mr. Foster leaned against his desk. "That last part wandered, but the heart of it works. You used the soliloquy."

As they sat down, Zaiden whispered, "So the audience is the one person she'd never want listening."

"Exactly," Owen said. "And we're all out there in the dark, hearing everything."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
Hayden balanced the microscope case on his knee while the school bus transported him, Francois and Macy out past the last stop, to the pond where Ms. Brown had set up a folding table with two slides, tweezers, and a jar of onion pieces. "Deadline's four o'clock," she said, checking her watch. "You have to draw and label one clean onion skin cell before the light goes. Cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. All three, or no credit."

Hayden's stomach tightened. Last year he had skipped the microscope unit entirely, faking a stomach ache because Francois said the lenses gave you headaches like propaganda, just rumours spread to scare people off, but Hayden had believed him anyway. Now here he was with three hours and no idea what he was looking for.

He peeled a tissue-thin layer of onion skin with the tweezers, dropped it onto the slide, and pressed on the cover slip too hard. It skidded off and floated away. Macy laughed without looking up from her own slide. "Gentle," she said. "It's delicate, not a sandwich." He tried again, slower, and this time the layer stayed flat. Through the lens at first he saw nothing but grey fog, then he nudged the fine focus and the fog broke into boxes, a grid of neat rectangles pressed edge to edge like a brick wall.

"That outline, the rigid part, that's the cell wall," Francois said over his shoulder, pointing at Hayden's drawing. Hayden traced it, then added the thin darker line just inside it and labelled the membrane. But the third label, the nucleus, was nowhere. He scanned row after row of empty rectangles and began to wonder if the dark spot was one of those things teachers invented, invisible in real life, like the headache rumour he'd fallen for before.

Then Macy made a small triumphant noise. "Found it. Little dark blob, off to the side." She squinted at it, tapping the slide with one finger. "Who even noticed that thing first? Somebody had to look at plant cells and decide the blob mattered." Francois shrugged, but Hayden remembered something from the book he'd skimmed on the bus, the one he'd read because he'd owed himself that much after last year. "The Scottish botanist Robert Brown," he said. "1831. He described the cell nucleus while he was studying orchid cells." Macy wrote it in the margin of her drawing. "Cool. Blobs with a history."

Hayden went back to his own slide. He reasoned that if the nucleus was real, it had to be in his cells too, just maybe out of view, so he moved the slide in slow, steady increments, a millimetre at a time, watching each new row of bricks slide past. On the third pass, near the corner of the tissue, a dark spot sat quietly inside one rectangle. He drew it, labelled it, and looked up at the pond light turning gold on the water. "Done," he said, and turned the microscope toward Francois. "Your turn. Don't believe anything I say about headaches."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
The group chat lit up at four thirty, right after school, with a photo from Wali. It showed a banner hanging over a table at the cultural festival on Saturday: navy cloth with silver thread spelling out one word, diaspora. Beneath it, Wali had typed, "My amma made this for our table but she went home with a headache and NONE of us knows what it says. Help??"

Ellie sat on her bed with her phone and studied the picture. She knew dias was something from math, like the distance across a circle, but this word had more letters. Donovan replied first with a shrug emoji and "some kind of festival thing?" which told her nothing. Then he added, "My table last year just said JAMAICA in big letters, everybody got it instantly." Wali answered, "Amma doesn't do anything without a reason. If she sewed this word, it matters." Ellie read the thread twice and made up her mind. She typed, "Don't take it down. Give me one hour."

She started with what she could see. The banner hung over a table of food, maps, and a photo album, and the album was open to a picture of Wali's great-grandparents standing in front of a house that was definitely not in this town, maybe not on this continent. Ellie thought about her own kitchen, where her mom kept a jar of pebbles from a beach her grandmother used to walk in Ireland, a beach none of them had ever seen. People carried places with them. Maybe the word was about that. But guessing wasn't knowing, so she looked it up in the big dictionary on the hallway shelf, the one nobody was allowed to consume snacks anywhere near. She ran her finger down the column, found the word, and read the entry twice to be sure she had it exactly.

Then she typed it into the chat herself: "Diaspora. From a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." She added, "I checked. That's the whole thing." Donovan sent back, "scattering, like seeds?" and Ellie typed, "Exactly like seeds. Blown everywhere, still the same plant." Wali went quiet for a minute, which in a group chat feels long, and then he said, "So the banner means my family isn't just from here. It means we're from somewhere, and we scattered, and we're still us." Ellie watched the typing dots appear and vanish twice before he finished: "I was going to swap the banner for one that just says where we live now. Forget that. Amma knew what she was doing."

On Saturday, Ellie rode her bike to the festival and found the table with the navy banner still hanging. Wali handed her a paper cup of milk tea and said, "I told every single person who stopped what the word means. This one lady said she'd never heard it before and now she can't stop saying it." Donovan showed up later with his little brother, pointed at the banner, and said, "That word means scattering, but like, the good kind," and Wali laughed and said, "Close enough." Ms. Brennan, who was running the bake sale two tables over, came by for tea and told a long anecdote about her own grandmother's recipe box, and by the end of it half the table was leaning in, telling their own stories. Ellie thought the day felt like the opposite of impoverished; it was crowded with things.

At closing time, Wali folded the banner gently, the way you fold a flag. "Amma texted," he said. "She wants to know who figured it out." Ellie pointed her thumb at herself. "Tell her a friend who looked it up," she said, "and tell her the banner is staying."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
story:
Isla knelt in the grass beside her three tomato pots, notebook damp against her knee, and glared at the fence. Something invisible was getting into her backyard at night and nibbling the lower leaves, and she intended to find out what.

"You're doing the stare method again," said Edmond, arriving through the side gate with a bag of pretzels. "It didn't work yesterday."

"It's not staring, it's observing." Behind Edmond came Aya, carrying Isla's crumpled science fair poster, which read, in enormous letters, PLANTS LIKE MUSIC. Mr. Zhu had looked at it for a long moment and asked, "How would you test that?" Isla had gone home, torn the poster in half, and started over. Now she had a better idea, and it started with the nibbled leaves.

"My mom calls it a hypothesis," Aya said, smoothing the poster on the picnic table. "A hypothesis is a testable guess."

"Right, and you write it like 'If ..., then ...'," Isla said. "You name the change you're making, and the result you predict." She wrote in her notebook: If I set out a plate of sunflower seeds near the fence, then the mystery nibbler will eat the seeds instead of my tomatoes. Edmond read it over her shoulder and nodded slowly, munching.

They set the plate by the fence at dusk, and the consequence was immediate and disgusting: by morning, the seeds were gone, a line of tiny footprints crossed the damp soil, and one fat squirrel sat on the fence transmitting pure smugness in Isla's direction. "It was you," she said. Edmond laughed so hard he knocked over the watering can.

But her hypothesis wasn't finished, because the tomatoes were still nibbled the next night, seeds and all. She tried again: If I cover only the tomatoes with netting, then the nibbling will stop. By morning the netted plants were untouched and the uncovered sunflowers along the fence were chewed to stubs. "It's the squirrel," Aya said, "but it could also be rabbits, honestly." Isla grinned and started a new page. Getting the wrong answer first wasn't a failure; it was data. Six trials later, Mr. Zhu leaned over the fence, studied her chart of footprints and bite marks, and raised an eyebrow.

"So," he said. "What's next?"

"Coyotes," said Edmond.

"Coyotes are not inevitable," said Isla, and clipped another piece of netting.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
Jaxon opened the group chat at 7:58 a.m. and read the message from Lola three times before typing anything.

"Science presentations start today. Mr. Somsak says every group presents, no exceptions."

His thumbs hovered. Last month he had told Mr. Somsak his stomach hurt and gotten out of the bee presentation. Before that, he had claimed his internet died during the English slideshow, which was easier because the whole class was online. He typed, then deleted, then typed again.

"not feeling great. tell Mr. Somsak I'll go tomorrow maybe."

Eric answered fast. "you said that last time and the time before." A pause, then another bubble. "I'll cover for you but you owe me. I want to do the microbe section anyway, the part about how bees carry them flower to flower. It's actually cool."

Lola's message came in slower. "Jaxon we practiced Sunday. you knew your part. what happened?"

He didn't answer. He muted the chat, put his phone face down on his bed, and pulled the blanket over his head. His whole body felt loose with relief, like dropping a heavy backpack. He even fell back asleep for an hour.

At lunch he unmuted the chat just to check. There were eleven messages. Lola had sent a photo of the class diagram, the one showing how bees pollinate the sparse desert flowers they'd studied, the ones that bloom only when a bee finds them. His slide. Someone else had filled it in.

"Mr. Somsak noticed you were gone again," Eric wrote. "he asked if everything's ok. not in a mean way."

Then a private message, just from Lola. "can I be honest? you skipped once and it helped. then you skipped again. did it get easier or harder? because from out here it looks harder."

Jaxon stared at the question. He thought about the first time, in the fall, when he'd only felt shaky for one afternoon afterward. The second time, the shakiness had lasted two days. Now, this morning, just reading the word "presentation" had made his chest tight before he'd even decided anything. The pattern was there, plain as the class diagram: every time he avoided it, the next one scared him more, not less.

He typed back, "harder. I just figured that out."

"so what if it's like the flowers," Lola wrote. "they only open when the bee actually shows up. you've never once seen yourself do the presentation, so your brain has no proof you can."

Jaxon sat with that. Tomorrow there was one more presentation slot, for groups doing extra credit. He could sign up. Or he could let the relief win again, and the one after that would be worse. He was still deciding, and he hated deciding.

He opened the chat, found the extra credit sign-up link, and typed his name in the box before he could delete it. His thumb shook a little on the send button.

"There," he said out loud, alone in his room. "Now I have to actually show up."

Lola replied with one word: "finally."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Brayden sat on his bed with the family group chat open on his mom's old phone. The dance was in four hours, and he had typed and deleted the same message six times.

"I don't know how to dance," he finally sent.

His aunt replied first, as usual. "Nobody does. That's the trick."

Then his eccentric uncle, the one who kept ferrets and a telescope on the roof, sent a link. "Watch this before you leave. It changed my whole life philosophy."

The video showed a white bird with a yellow crest on its head, bobbing and stepping as a song played. His uncle's message followed: "In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed."

"A bird," Brayden typed back.

"A bird," his uncle confirmed.

Brayden watched it three more times. Snowball wasn't doing anything fancy. He bounced on one foot, then the other, then shook his head, and when the song slowed down, the bird slowed down too, still landing on the beat. Brayden had an idea, and since there was nobody in the kitchen to watch him fail, he decided to test it there. He put on a song, bounced on one foot, then the other, then shook his head. When the tempo changed, he counted the new beat in his head and adjusted, just like the cockatoo had. It wasn't pretty. But it matched.

At the dance, the gym smelled like floor wax and somebody's older brother's cologne. Yasser was already near the wall, holding a cup of punch like a shield. Lea-Maude stood next to him, doing a small side-to-side step that didn't touch any beat at all.

"Lea-Maude," Brayden said. "Try bouncing. One foot, then the other. And when the song speeds up, you speed up."

"Why?"

"Because it works. I tested it."

She squinted at him, then tried it. On the fourth bounce, she landed exactly with the kick drum, and her whole face changed. "It works," she said, sounding personally offended that nobody had told her sooner.

The DJ put on a slow song and half the gym froze, but Brayden counted the new, slower tempo in his head and slowed his bounce to match. Lea-Maude did the same. Yasser set down his punch and joined them, mostly on beat.

Ms. Rao, on chaperone duty by the door, watched them for a moment. "Where did you three learn that?"

"Family group chat," Brayden said.

"An uncle," Lea-Maude added, still bouncing. "The eccentric one, probably."

"He mentored a cockatoo," Brayden said, which wasn't exactly true, but the beat dropped and there was no time to fix it.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: When a number inside a summed range changes, the SUM formula recalculates the total automatically.
story:
Henry had one class period to get the spreadsheet right, because Mr. Addo had promised that the student with the cleanest budget chart would run the announcement screen at the spring concert. That was the job Henry wanted more than anything, standing at the controls in front of the whole school, so he had claimed the computer next to the window and started typing numbers into column B: what the drama club would spend on costumes, paint, and programs.

"You're doing it all by hand?" Avani asked, leaning over from the next seat. She wanted her chart to have the tallest bars in the room, even if she had to pick categories that made the club look rich. "Mr. Addo said there's a faster way."

Henry typed an equals sign, then SUM, then dragged his cursor down the column of costs. When he pressed Enter, the total appeared at the bottom like it had been waiting there the whole time. "Cool," he said, but he did not trust it. The number looked too big, forty dollars too big, and he could not see why. The formula was hiding whatever was wrong, the way a closed locker hides a mess.

He thought about that for a minute, tapping his pencil on the desk while the lab's old fan rattled in the corner. If the formula really was adding the whole column, then changing any single number ought to change the total too. So he tested it. He clicked on the paint cost, changed 25 to 26, and watched the total jump up by exactly one dollar, all by itself, without him touching the SUM at all. Then he changed it back, and the total dropped again. The formula was working. That meant the problem was in one of the numbers themselves.

He scrolled down the column, one cell at a time, checking each entry against the crumpled budget sheet in his pocket. Near the bottom he found it: the programs cost, which should have read 15, had an extra digit typed after it. He fixed the typo, and the total shrank by forty dollars on its own, instantly, before he even breathed.

"Whoa," Avani said, peering over. "It fixed itself." She looked at her own chart, where she had been padding the decoration budget to make her bars taller, and her shoulders dropped a little. "Maybe mine should just show the real numbers too." Behind them, Mr. Addo paused on his way past and smiled at the screen, mentioning to another teacher that he had built a spreadsheet just like it to watch his own pension after a few volatile years in the market, and that charts helped him sleep at night. Henry highlighted his corrected column, clicked the bar chart button, and watched eight gray bars rise across the screen. "Now label the axes," Avani said, "and then we submit both at the same time."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
story:
The cast on Lily's right arm still felt like a stranger, stiff and heavy, and the doctor's words kept circling back to her all week: a fracture of the radius near the wrist, the most common fracture seen in children. She had heard the nurse say it almost cheerfully, as if Lily had joined an enormous club. Now she sat on the low wall by the basketball court, watching Mattea roll her borrowed skateboard back and forth across the cracked pavement.

"I want to learn the kick turn today," Mattea said, pushing off again. "I don't care how many times I stack it. I'll persevere until I get it." Her shoelaces were double-knotted and she'd drawn a tiny flame on the grip tape with marker, because the flame meant the board was equivalent to a race car, at least in her head. Lily suspected nothing could make a wobbly plastic skateboard equivalent to a race car, but she kept that to herself.

"Mattea, wait," Lily said. "How did I break mine?" She held up the cast. "Think about it. I didn't land on my elbow or my shoulder."

Mattea stopped, one foot on the tail of the board. "You put your hands out. You skidded on both palms and then the right one kind of folded."

"Exactly. Falling onto an outstretched hand. That's what does it." Lily stood, warming to the puzzle. She had been turning it over for days, the way you turn over a rock to see what lives underneath. Every skater she could remember falling at the park had done the same thing, hands shooting forward like springs. Was it a rule, then? Did hands always jump out first? "Let's test it. Fall down. On purpose. Softly, onto the grass."

Mattea flopped onto the grass beside the court, arms at her sides, and bounced a little. "Feels weird. My hands wanted to go out even when I knew I was falling."

"I know! Mine too, the whole ride down." Lily noticed Mr. Munro across the yard, winding up the long jump rope for the younger kids, and waved him over. "Mr. Munro, when kids fall off things here, do they mostly catch themselves with their hands?"

He thought for a second, then nodded. "Almost always. Outstretched hands. The wrist pays for it."

"That's what I thought," Lily said. So the rule held even off the board, even on monkey bars and scooters and the icy patch by the doors every January. The hidden cause wasn't the skateboard at all. It was the landing.

"Okay, new plan," Mattea said, brushing grass off her knees. "Teach me to fall on my forearms instead."

They practiced on the grass for the whole recess, Mattea dropping and rolling, tucking her hands in, getting stranger and faster at it. On her last try she landed smooth as a cat and popped straight up.

"Now the kick turn," she said, and stepped onto the board.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
Nevaeh stood in Mr. Nur's kitchen with a list of emergency numbers on the fridge and a six-month-old baby on her shoulder, and the baby was screaming like a smoke alarm with opinions. Mr. Nur had left twenty minutes ago for a parent thing at the school, and Nevaeh had already tried bouncing, singing, and a sock puppet named Gerald, who was now sweating from the effort.

The baby's face had gone a dark tomato red. Nevaeh paced the hallway, past the framed photos of Mr. Nur's family and a shelf of shells arranged by size. She thought about her baby-sitting course, the Saturday one with the plastic dolls. The instructor had said something she hadn't fully believed at the time: shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head. Nevaeh had thought, that seems extreme, it's just a little jiggle. But she remembered the instructor's flat, serious voice, and the way the whole room had gone quiet.

She was not going to shake the baby. Obviously. But her arms were doing an impulsive little frustrated bounce without asking her permission, so she made a decision instead. She carried the baby to the crib in the nursery, laid him down on his back, checked that the blanket was below his arms, and stepped out into the hallway. She closed the door halfway and stood there breathing.

Through the gap she could hear the crying continue, drop a little, then continue. She sat on the hallway floor beside a potted plant that was definitely fake, because it had dust on its leaves. "Okay," she whispered. "Think." Crying meant something. Babies didn't cry for no reason, the instructor had said, and Nevaeh decided she could infer the cause if she collected clues like a detective. Not hungry, she'd tried a bottle. Diaper, checked twice, both times heroic. Not tired, because he'd slept before Mr. Nur left.

Then she remembered the sock. When she'd checked the diaper the second time, one sock had been off, and she'd thought nothing of it. But when she took it off, had there been something inside? She crept back into the nursery. The baby was still red-faced but the cries had become grumbly, hiccupy ones. Nevaeh picked up the sock and shook it gently over her palm. A folded hospital bracelet fell out, and a long blond hair, wrapped around the baby's actual sock underneath had been a tiny plastic hospital tag with sharp edges. She hadn't felt it through the sock.

She slid the tag out from the sock, held it up to the lamp, and winced. It had a corner like a shark fin. "Buddy," she said, "you've been walking on a shark this whole time." The baby blinked at her with wet eyelashes and made a sound like a small question.

She freed the hair, removed the tag, put the sock back on, and lifted him up, careful to cup her hand behind his head the way the instructor had drilled into them. He gave one last hiccup and then, insultingly fast, fell asleep against her collarbone, leaving a warm wet patch on her shirt. When Mr. Nur came home an hour later, he found Nevaeh on the couch with the baby asleep in the crib and the plastic tag held up in triumph. "I'd like to open negotiations regarding my fee," she said, "because I solved a mystery."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Noah had been carrying his grandfather's watch in his jacket pocket for three days, wrapped in a paper towel so it would not get scratched. Now he stood at the edge of the cemetery with Wali and Hendrik on either side of him, and the cold came up through his shoes. His mother and aunts stood closer to the grave, near the flowers. Noah kept his hand in his pocket, touching the watch the way you keep checking for your phone, except this was heavier and older and had stopped at 4:17.

"Are you going to put it on?" Wali asked, watching him.

"I don't know." That was the honest answer. He had read somewhere that you were supposed to let go, move on, get back to normal, and part of him wondered whether wearing a dead person's watch every day was the opposite of that. Maybe it was like refusing to believe it happened. His cousin had said grief was contagious, that if you held on to things too tight, everyone around you caught the sadness and nobody got better. Noah had no way to verify that. He could not exactly run an experiment on his whole family.

After the service, people drifted toward the cars, but Ms. Demetriou, who lived two doors down and had known his grandfather from the chess club at the library, stayed behind with him. She saw him turning the watch over in his palm. "I used to think keeping my father's things meant I was stuck," she said. "Then a counsellor handed me a book. Continuing Bonds, from 1996. It argued that keeping a connection to someone who died, through memories, objects, traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. Not the opposite of it." She shrugged. "I still make his soup every October."

Noah looked down at the watch. So it was not a rule that you had to drop everything and walk away. It was more like a probability: some ways of remembering helped, some probably did not, and wearing a watch that made him think of Saturday chess games seemed likely to be one of the good ones. He buckled it on. It was loose around his wrist, so loose it slid almost to his elbow, and Hendrik laughed and said it looked like a bracelet on a fence post.

"Give it two years," Noah said. "I'll grow into it."

They walked back along the gravel path together, and every few steps the watch slipped down and Noah pushed it up again, the small metal circle catching the low winter sun.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
story:
Lea stood at the steel prep counter behind the restaurant's kitchen, an onion in front of her and a knife that had seen better days. On the counter lay a note in Ms. Dhillon's looping handwriting, left there before the dinner rush: "Sauce needs six onions, diced small. If they make you cry, remember the goggles in the drawer." At the bottom, she had added a second line. "Kenneth wants his pasta special on Saturday's menu. Tell him yes or no by five." Lea folded the note into her apron pocket, because Kenneth was already hovering by the stove, waiting for her answer like the sauce depended on it, which in a way it did.

"The special is my recipe," Kenneth said. "My grandmother's. I just need someone to chop proper onion for it. Hamza said he'd stir, but he's voluntary help only, he keeps reminding me." That was true. Hamza had wandered in from the alley, announced he was there voluntarily, and stationed himself by the pot with a wooden spoon.

Lea curled her fingers into the claw grip Ms. Dhillon had shown her, knuckles forward, fingertips tucked away, and pressed down on the onion. The knife slid off without cutting. She pressed harder. It skated sideways again and nearly caught her knuckle, and her breath went shallow. She turned the blade toward the light and saw how the edge had gone dull and rounded, worn down by a year of chopping. Her mind went to the drawer of knives by the sink, the one Ms. Dhillon kept for the sharp ones. If a dull knife needed all that pushing, then a sharp one must need less, and a knife you barely push cannot slip. She fetched a slim blade with a fine edge, and it sank through the onion like the onion wanted it to.

"I'm switching to this one," she said, holding it up. "A sharp knife is safer than a dull one. It needs less pressure, so it won't slip off the food."

"Safer," Hamza repeated, dubious, watching her from the pot.

"Safer," Lea said, and went back to work. The onion dwindled from a whole bulb to a neat pile of even dice, and her eyes barely stung. She swept the pieces into the pan where the oil shimmered, and Kenneth added the tomatoes his grandmother would have used, crushed by hand.

"So," he said, spoon in midair. "Saturday? Yes or no? It's five o'clock somewhere."

Lea wiped the blade, laid it flat, and gave the sauce one slow stir. "Yes," she said. "Tell your grandmother her recipe made the menu."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel, with its two leads touching either end of the component being tested.
story:
Muhammad crouched at the electronics bench in the science museum's lower lab, a coil of thin wire in front of him, a battery, a voltmeter, and an ammeter clipped into a tidy circuit. The worksheet on the clipboard asked for one number: the resistance of the wire. All he had to do was measure the voltage across it and the current through it, then divide. Simple, except that the voltmeter kept reading zero.

"Your leads are wrong," Brooklyn said, leaning over his shoulder. "You have to put the voltmeter in line, like the ammeter. Break the circuit and stick it in."

"That can't be right," Muhammad said. "If we break the circuit, the current stops, and then what are we even measuring?" He scrutinized the diagram taped to the bench, a drawing of a battery, a resistor, and two meters. In the picture, the ammeter sat inside the loop, but the voltmeter hovered outside it, connected by its own two little branches. The drawing looked almost lazy, as if whoever made it had forgotten to draw the meter into the circuit properly. Muhammad ran his finger along the lines twice.

Tamara plugged in the battery and the ammeter jumped to life, showing 0.5 amps. So current was flowing. The voltmeter, still reading zero, must be sitting in a dead spot. "In the drawing," Muhammad said slowly, "the voltmeter's leads touch the two ends of the resistor. Not the middle, not the battery. Just the two ends."

He unclipped the red lead and the black lead and moved them so each one touched a different end of the wire, the voltmeter now attached alongside it in its own separate path. The needle swung over and settled at 1.5 volts. "There," he said. "So the voltmeter measures voltage when it's connected in parallel, with its two leads touching either end of the thing you're testing."

"Parallel," Tamara repeated, writing it down. "Okay. Divide."

Muhammad did the math. 1.5 divided by 0.5 was 3 ohms. Then he remembered last summer at his cousin's house, when the porch light kept dimming and his uncle had traced the wire along the railing, hunting for a bad section he couldn't see. His uncle had said the wire would tell on itself if you measured it right. At the time Muhammad had thought that was just something grown-ups said. Now it seemed almost literal. You couldn't see resistance, but the two numbers together gave it away, like footprints.

They tested a second wire, a thicker one with a colorful polymer coating, and got a smaller number, 1 ohm. Brooklyn tried the leads himself, placing them correctly on the first try, and grinned when the needle moved.

Ms. Toussaint wandered by, glanced at their worksheet, and slid a granola bar onto the bench beside Muhammad. "You three missed the lunch talk," she said. "That's nutritious and you earned it."

Muhammad pocketed it and copied the last number onto the sheet in his neatest writing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
Isabelle had volunteered at the soup kitchen for exactly forty minutes, and already she had a mystery. Every Saturday, she had learned from the schedule taped to the fridge, a van arrived with crates of fresh vegetables, carrots still muddy, apples with leaves still clinging to their stems. Fresh produce was expensive. The soup kitchen's budget was small. So where did it all come from? She asked the woman who ran the kitchen, but the woman only shrugged and said, "Ask the driver, hon."

The driver was a college kid with a stable of canvas totes in the back of his van, all labeled with the name of a farm. Isabelle wanted to ask him, but every time she got close, he was already halfway out the door. She decided to verify her first guess, that a rich person donated the money and the kitchen bought the produce. She checked the donation binder by the register. There were plenty of donors, but none big enough for weekly crates of vegetables, and the kitchen's produce orders were all frozen and canned. So her first idea was wrong. Whatever was happening, it wasn't money. It was something else, some rule she hadn't figured out yet.

She wasn't the only one working the mystery. Julien, who had been coming since September, wanted to win the kitchen's volunteer-of-the-month photo on the lobby wall more than anything. He was sure the secret was a famous person who didn't want attention, and he kept trying to peek at the driver's paperwork. "If I find out who it is," Julien whispered, "they'd put my picture up for solving it."

When the van pulled up that Saturday, Isabelle was ready. She carried a crate of potatoes so heavy she had to set it down twice, and she made a point of turning it over. The label didn't say a store or a warehouse. It said Field 4. Potatoes do not come from Field 4 of a store. They come from a farm, and only from a farm, after a harvest.

Her friend Ananya, who had rushed in late from a morning audition for the school play and was still humming her song under her breath, lifted a carrot and frowned at its broken top. "These look like leftovers," Ananya said. "My uncle does this. It's called gleaning. Gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks."

Isabelle stared at the potatoes, dirt still on them, several of them nicked and small, the kind a machine would leave behind. That was the pattern. Not perfect vegetables bought with money. Leftover vegetables picked by hand, by volunteers, the machines having passed over them already. She turned to the driver as he hefted the last crate.

"Do you pick these yourself?" she asked.

"Every Saturday," he said. "You two want to come out next weekend? We could use more hands. Bring gloves."

Julien was already reaching for the signup sheet. "Sign me up twice," he said, and Isabelle laughed and wrote her name right below his.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
Jacob had until eight o'clock tomorrow morning to make his science fair project work, and all he had was a water rocket with a sticky piston and a launch pad stuck in the backyard grass. The rocket refused to fly. He pumped and pumped, but the piston jammed halfway up the tube every single time.

Amalia sat on the porch steps eating a banana, and that was the start of the real trouble. "You have flies all over you," Jacob said, swatting the air. "It's the banana," Amalia said. "Rotting fruit just makes them. Everybody knows that. Leave a peach out and boom, fruit flies, straight out of the peach." Jacob stared at her. "Out of the peach? They crawl out of it?" "They appear," Amalia said, like it was obvious.

Jacob went inside and called Fatimah, who owned every book about scientists in the school library. She read to him over the phone, slow and clear: "In 1668, Francesco Redi put meat in jars. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat." Jacob wrote it down on his hand because he couldn't find paper. "So if the flies can't get to the rotting stuff," he said, "nothing shows up." "That's Redi," Fatimah said. "You should test it. That's the whole point of a hypothesis. It's a guess you can actually check, and the check can go either way." Jacob looked at the clock. Seven hours until the bus.

He modified his plan fast. Forget the rocket. He set up three jars on the backyard picnic table: one open with a slice of Amalia's banana, one sealed tight with a slice inside, and one covered with gauze held by a rubber band, flies kept off but air getting in. Amalia stood over it with her arms crossed. "This is a counterfeit experiment," she said. "Nothing's going to happen in the sealed one anyway, so what does that prove?" "Then you have nothing to worry about," Jacob said.

At six in the morning, in the gray light, they crouched over the table. The open jar had four tiny flies walking on the banana. The sealed jar had nothing, and Amalia said, "Fine, but that's just because it's airtight." Then Jacob lifted the gauze. Nothing. Not one fly, not one speck, on banana that was brown and soft and as rotten as the first one. Amalia leaned so close her nose almost touched the glass. She looked at the gauze, then at Jacob, then at the gauze again. "Okay," she said quietly. "Okay, fine. They come from outside." Jacob grabbed the jar, the notebook, and the gauze, and ran for the bus.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
Muhammad held the onion like it was a live grenade. "If I cry, don't tell anyone at school," he said.

Brynn's grandmother, Ms. Tang, had declared it Cooking Day at her house, which meant Brynn, Muhammad, and Maci were making pasta sauce from scratch while she supervised from a lawn chair in the kitchen. She was famously eccentric; she drank tea out of a measuring cup and wore a sun hat indoors. "Bend your fingers under, like a claw," she said. "Knuckles forward. The knife slides past them, never toward them."

Muhammad curled his fingers, knuckles bumping the blade as it cut through the onion. Slice, slice, slice. His eyes stung a little, but no tears, and nothing resembled a trip to the emergency room.
