Maci applauded with a wooden spoon in each hand. He had offered to be Muhammad's tutor for the afternoon, mostly by shouting "CLAW!" whenever Muhammad's thumb drifted.

The sauce came together in the pan: onion, canned tomatoes, a pinch of sugar, salt. Then Muhammad noticed a problem. The sauce was thin and watery, sliding around the pan like a red puddle instead of coating anything. "This is going to drip right off the noodles," he said, frowning at it.

Meanwhile Brynn was draining the pasta over the sink, steam billowing up like a stage effect. Maci lunged across the kitchen and grabbed the pot before the last of the water vanished. "Wait! Save a cup," she said, scooping some of the cloudy liquid into a mug. Muhammad stared at it. The water looked almost milky, which was strange, since it had started out clear. He reasoned that the pasta must have released starch into it while it cooked, and he had read somewhere that starch could make liquids thicker. He tested the idea slowly, splashing a little of the starchy water into the pan and stirring. The sauce tightened around his spoon. He added a splash more, and it clung, glossy and thick, exactly the way sauce was supposed to.

The twist came at dinner. Ms. Tang took one bite, removed her sun hat, and saluted Muhammad with her fork. "Better than the restaurant on Bridge Street," she declared. Muhammad was so proud he stood up and did a small bow, which was a mistake, because his knee hit the table and his fork launched a meatball across the kitchen. It landed, improbably, in the measuring cup of tea.

Brynn looked at the floating meatball, then at Muhammad. "Grandma drinks that," she warned.

Ms. Tang sipped anyway. "Mmm," she said. "Needs more sauce."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Emmett opened the laptop at the kitchen table and found the group chat already buzzing. Three messages from Lilah about the science project, one from Fraser, and then, near the bottom, his own name in a line he had typed an hour ago and forgotten: EMMETT WHERE IS YOUR SLIDE. He had meant it as a reminder to himself, typed into the wrong window in a hurry before dinner, and now it sat there like something dropped in the middle of the room.

Lilah replied first. "why are you yelling?" Then Fraser: "lol emmett calm down." Emmett stared at the screen. Yelling? He hadn't said a word out loud all evening. He read the message again, then read theirs, and a gradual understanding started to form, the way a picture comes up when you turn a Polaroid over. His words were in capital letters, every single one, and somehow that made them read like a shout even though they were just pixels on a screen.

He started to type "I wasn't yelling," stopped, and tried to presume nothing about what they'd understood. Instead he typed it the way he actually felt: "sorry. my little cousin was hammering the keyboard and I didn't check before I sent it. the slide is done, it's the volcano diagram." He kept everything lowercase and calm on purpose, testing whether the letters themselves changed how the message landed.

"ok good," Lilah wrote. Fraser sent a thumbs up. It seemed settled, but it wasn't, because underneath their messages sat one from Mr. Walker, sent to the whole class an hour ago: REMEMBER, PRESENTATIONS BEGIN AT NINE TOMORROW. NO EXCEPTIONS. Emmett felt his stomach tighten. He scrolled back through weeks of messages, looking for the pattern he half suspected was there. Every message from Mr. Walker was in capitals. Every single one, all year, like a wall of loud.

Then came the twist. Lilah typed, "wait. mr. walker never types like that. check the name." Emmett looked closer. The sender was Mr. Walker's name, sure enough, but the email address behind it was a jumble of numbers, not the school address they'd all seen on the syllabus. "Someone's using his name," Fraser wrote. "my mom says that happens. fake accounts copy real ones." The three of them sat in their separate houses, and Emmett could almost feel them all leaning toward their screens at once.

He opened a new message and typed to the real Mr. Walker, using the address from the syllabus, being careful to keep his own letters quiet and ordinary: "Hi Mr. Walker, someone is messaging our class using your name in all caps. We think it's fake. Should we tell the office?" He pressed send and watched the screen, the cursor blinking, the house quiet around him except for the fridge humming in the corner.

The reply came in four minutes, in ordinary lowercase, patient and plain. "Good catch, Emmett. Tell the office tonight. And thanks for not shouting about it." Emmett grinned, screenshotted everything, and reached for his shoes.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Cooked rice can rest off the heat with the lid on for several minutes, which lets the trapped steam finish cooking it and frees the stove for other dishes.
story:
The kitchen at her grandmother's house smelled like toasted cumin, and Lea had exactly one hour to get rice, curry, and flatbread on the table at the same time. Her grandmother had twisted her ankle chasing a squirrel off the tomato plants, so she sat by the window giving directions, while Lea did the actual cooking for the first time. Riya had come along, partly to help and partly because she wanted to learn flatbread, since her cousins joked that nobody in her family could make it without turning it into a cracker. "Watch," Riya said, holding up a rolling pin like a knight's sword. "Today I break the stereotype of Riya's flatbread shame."

The rice came to a boil first, so Lea turned the burner down low and started on the curry, chopping onions until her eyes stung. Then the timer went off. "It's done already?" she said, staring at the pot. The rice had absorbed all the water, but the grains still looked slightly firm at the centers when she pinched one. The curry needed another ten minutes, and the flatbread hadn't even been rolled. She pictured the whole meal collapsing like a bad science project. "Grandma, the rice is early and everything else is late."

"Don't panic," her grandmother said from the window. "Think it through."

Lea looked at the pot, at the two burners she had left, at Riya already dusting the counter with flour. The problem wasn't the rice being done. The problem was that she only had two burners and three dishes orbiting them like planets around a too-small sun. Then she noticed something. When she lifted the lid to check the rice, steam billowed out and fogged the window above the stove, leaving it translucent until she wiped it away. There was steam trapped in there. Steam was heat, sort of. Maybe the rice could keep going somewhere else.

She slid the pot onto the cold back corner of the stove and clamped the lid down tight. "What if it just sits there?" she said. "With the lid on. Off the heat." Riya raised an eyebrow but kept rolling her dough into a circle that was more of a lopsided oval. "If you say so. My job is the flatbread."

For ten minutes Lea stirred the curry and watched Riya slap dough onto the hot pan. The first one puffed up like a balloon, and Riya actually did a small victory dance with the spatula. "Tell my cousins," she announced. "Tell everyone." The second one puffed too. When everything was ready, Lea lifted the rice lid, braced for disappointment, and found the grains plump and separate, perfectly cooked all the way through.

They carried the dishes to the table where her grandmother waited, and the old woman leaned over the rice pot and breathed in. "So," she said, spooning some onto her plate, "you figured out the rice rests off the heat with the lid on, and the steam finishes it while you cook the bread." Lea grinned and held up the last flatbread, still steaming. "One pot, one pan, one timing," she said. "Riya, take a picture of that bread before it disappears."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
Jonathan pushed his peas around his plate while his father asked the usual dinner questions, and he gave the usual answers, until his father said, "You're doing the thing with the peas again. That means something happened."

"Mr. Georgiou had a garage sale," Jonathan said. "He had a box of old hockey cards. One of them was a Rocco Vale rookie card."

His mother set down her fork. "The one you've wanted since March?"

"The one that was forty dollars at the card shop. Mr. Georgiou wanted ten for it." Jonathan had stood in the driveway holding his allowance, and he had not bought it. That was the part that still hurt. "I offered eight. He said no. I said I'd think about it, and Lola's brother bought it for ten like two minutes later."

His father winced. "Rough."

"There's another one," Jonathan said quickly. "Tayla told me her cousin has one and doesn't even like hockey. She's asking around."

The next day Tayla met him by the fence. "Bad news. My cousin wants twenty. She found out there's a whole group of kids at Riverside who collect Rocco Vale now. Everybody wants that card and there's only, like, four in town."

Four cards, and by Jonathan's count at least nine kids who wanted one. He thought about the card shop, where the same card sat behind glass at forty dollars, unsold, for months. The shop had it, but nobody there was buying at that price. Ten dollars had worked in about two minutes. He chewed on that through math class, through dinner, through the peas.

By Saturday he had a plan, and by the following Saturday the plan had mostly involved waiting, which was the hard part. Then Tayla appeared at his door. "Guess what. Three more Rocco Vale cards turned up. Some guy cleaned out his attic and sold them all to the card shop, and the shop's got a stack now, and they dropped the price to fifteen. My cousin panicked and told me she'd take twelve."

Jonathan counted his money. He had eleven dollars and a jar of coins worth about two more. "Tell her eleven fifty," he said, "or she can watch the shop price keep dropping." It was a gamble, and he knew it. But the cards were getting plentiful, and plentiful things got cheaper. He had watched it happen twice now, in both directions.

Tayla came back an hour later holding the card in a plastic sleeve. "She took eleven fifty. Also, she says you're 'annoyingly right.'"

At dinner that night his father asked what happened to the peas circling. "I got the card," Jonathan said, and set the sleeve on the table between the salt and the ketchup. His mother leaned in to admire it.

His father studied the card, then him. "So the price went down when there were more of them, and up when everybody wanted the few there were. You figured that out yourself?"

"Mr. Georgiou actually told me the name for it, after Lola's brother bought mine," Jonathan said. "When I went back to sulk at his sale. He said the price where buyers want exactly as many as sellers have is called the equilibrium price. Market-clearing price, he said. Whatever. I just call it the pea price." He ate a pea.

His mother raised an eyebrow at "whatever," since clearly he had gone home and written both terms in his notebook. Nobody at the table had to say that out loud.

The twist arrived on Tuesday. Tayla found him at his locker, holding her own Roco Vale card. "Riverside kids moved on. It's some gymnast now. Everyone's trading Vale cards away for nothing." She flipped the card into the air. Jonathan caught it against the locker door, agile for once.

He now owned two of a card that half the school was trying to sell. He put his forehead on the locker door and stayed there for a while.

"Some collector you are," Tayla said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
story:
The phone sat in the middle of the kitchen table like it might bolt if nobody watched it. Paige's dad slid it toward her with two fingers. "Before you touch it, we agree on the rules. Dinner hour is off. Homework first. And I can monitor the screen-time report every Sunday, so no surprises for either of us." Paige nodded so fast her ponytail bounced. She had waited two years for this, and she was not going to lose the phone over a rule on day one.

Her first text went to Charlotte: "Got it!!!" Three exclamation points felt right. Charlotte replied with a row of hearts. Then Paige tried Mael, whose family ran the feed store outside town. His answer came back: "cool. im not doing the agriculture thing." Paige stared at that. Not doing it how? Not doing the homework poster about farming, or not going to the agriculture club meeting, or quitting it forever? The message was ambiguous, and she caught herself inventing three different problems to worry about. She typed "which thing?" and set the phone face down while she waited.

Face down was her own idea. She had noticed, in the first hour, that every time the screen lit up, her eyes went to it even mid-sentence. So she ran a small test on herself: phone face down by the fruit bowl during homework, phone in her pocket after. When she checked later, she had finished her math in twenty minutes instead of her usual forty. "Huh," she said out loud, and wrote the result on a sticky note.

Mael finally answered. "the poster. im still in the club." Then he added, "did you know the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973?" Paige read it twice. Fifty-some years, and phones in pockets had been around that whole time? Her dad had told stories about waiting by the wall phone in the hallway as a kid, and now she understood why he had never once carried one to school. She looked it up on her new phone, which felt appropriate somehow, and the dates matched.

At dinner she reported everything: the screen-time plan, the face-down trick, the sticky note, Martin Cooper on his New York street in 1973. Her dad laughed until he had to put his fork down. "Text Mael that if a call ever goes that far again, it should at least be pizza related." Paige picked up the phone, then put it back down and picked up her fork first. Rules were rules.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
At the gathering after Grandma Dot's funeral, Rose counted the casseroles on the kitchen table and realized she had eaten exactly one forkful of food in two days. Her aunt pressed a plate of scalloped potatoes into her hands and said, "You need to eat, sweetheart." Rose tried. Her throat seemed to close around the second bite, like a door swinging shut.

She found her friends Tabitha and Micaela on the back porch steps. Tabitha had come with her mom, who knew Rose's mother from work, and Micaela lived three houses down and had simply walked over with a plate of cookies. "I think I'm getting sick," Rose told them quietly. "I haven't slept since Tuesday. Not really. And food tastes like paper towels." She laid it out like an equation: sick people can't sleep, sick people can't eat, therefore she must be sick. The math felt solid.

Micaela frowned. "But you don't have a fever or anything?" Rose shook her head. No fever, no sore throat, no cough. That was the strange part. She kept turning the problem over, the way she'd turn a puzzle cube, looking for the side she hadn't checked yet. Then she noticed something. Her uncle, the loud one who usually told three jokes before the soup even came out, was sitting alone in the corner with a full plate, chewing one bite and setting down his fork. Her mother had said she'd been up since four in the morning. Even Cousin Beatrix, who was twenty and usually ate like a horse, was just pushing rice around.

Rose went around the living room, doing a quiet survey. "How did you sleep last night?" she asked her uncle. "Terribly," he admitted. She asked her mother the same question, and got a tired laugh and the word "barely." Rose sat down on the stairs with her notebook and wrote the results in a column. Nearly everyone here was exhausted and not eating. They couldn't all be coming down with the same flu. So the cause had to be something they shared, something that wasn't a virus at all. What they shared was Grandma Dot. Grief, it seemed, wasn't only a feeling. It landed in the body too, dragging down sleep and appetite like a turbulent wind shoving a small boat off course. She had the whole fact now, tested on her own family.

Ms. Vu, who lived next door and had come by with a lemon cake, settled onto the step beside her. "You look like a scientist at work," she said. Rose showed her the column of tally marks. "I thought I was sick," Rose said, "but I don't think so anymore. I think this is what grief does." Ms. Vu nodded slowly and didn't try to reassure her with anything cheerful, which Rose appreciated more than she could say. Instead Ms. Vu said, "Then eating one bite is a victory, not a failure."

Rose looked at her abandoned plate. She picked up the fork and took another bite of potatoes, chewing carefully. It still tasted mostly like nothing, but she swallowed it anyway, and then one more after that. Across the room, her uncle picked up his fork too. Rose raised hers in the air like a tiny flag, and he grinned and raised his back.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A rainforest climate graph shows a nearly flat temperature line, because temperatures there stay warm and change little from month to month.
story:
Juliette spread the two graphs across the library table and pressed them flat with her pencil case so the fan in the corner wouldn't flip them over. One belonged to the desert, all jagged peaks and dips. The other belonged to the rainforest, and something about it made her frown.

"You're doing the climate project too?" Kael asked, sliding into the seat across from her. He shook rain off his jacket. "Mr. Hassan wants rainfall and temperature compared by Friday, right?"

"Right," Juliette said. "But look at this rainforest graph. I think the photocopier cut it off, or somebody drew the temperature line wrong." She tapped the paper. The temperature line ran almost flat, month after month, like a ruler laid across the page. "Nobody's temperature does that. Even our town goes up in summer and down in winter."

Kael leaned in and squinted. "Maybe it's a misprint. You should ask for another copy."

The bell rang before they could argue about it, and in the hallway Juliette found Timothy by the lockers. His family had come from a place with rainforest at the edge of it, and he kept a photo taped inside his locker door: green crowding up to the sky, mist hanging in the branches.

"Timothy, your heritage, the rainforest part," she said. "Is the weather there different every month, like here?"

He shrugged. "My grandmother writes to me about it. Read this." He pulled a folded letter from his backpack and handed it over. The paper was soft and worn, durable from being read so many times.

Juliette unfolded it. Warm again this month, the looping handwriting said. Warm last month, warm the month before. Your cousin swims in the river every day of the year. Juliette read it twice, then a third time, and her heart started to beat faster. She looked up at Timothy, and the flat line on the graph suddenly looked different.

"It's not a misprint," she said slowly. "The temperature line is flat because temperatures in a rainforest stay warm and change little from month to month. That's what the graph is supposed to look like."

"So you don't need another copy," Timothy said, grinning.

She borrowed the letter. Back at the table, she laid it beside the desert graph, where the temperature line climbed and crashed like a roller coaster, and she wrote her first sentence: The rainforest graph shows a nearly flat temperature line. Then she flipped the rainforest rainfall bars upward, tall and steady, so different from the desert's short stubs.

Kael came back and read over her shoulder. "You solved it with a letter?"

"My grandmother's letter," Timothy said from behind him. "Best source in the library."

Juliette laughed and underlined her sentence twice.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
story:
The stadium screen showed the crowd in the arena below, and above the seats a giant photograph depicted the Stanley Cup, silver and dented, with names carved in rings all the way down. Megan squinted at it. The trophy looked like something dug out of a grandparents' attic, not like a prize the best hockey team in the world would fight for.

"Why does it look so old?" Adriana asked, handing Megan a foam finger. "Don't they make a new one every year, like the Lombardi Trophy?"

Colt shook his head. "It's the same one every year. My dad says they pass it around. But I don't know why it's all banged up."

Megan wondered about that. Trophies she knew, the ones at school, were shiny and new because somebody had ordered them from a catalog. She thought about it while the crowd chanted. It couldn't be arbitrary, could it, some team just deciding to keep a beat-up old cup forever? There had to be a reason hidden somewhere, like a rule nobody had told her yet.

"I'm going to ask Mr. Zhu," she said. Their neighbour had a seat three rows down and knew more hockey trivia than the announcers did. She climbed over knees and popcorn, found him, and asked her question straight out. He laughed, pulled out his phone, and turned the screen toward her. "It was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892," he read, "and first awarded in 1893. Oldest trophy in North American professional sports."

Megan's eyes went wide. "Eighteen ninety-three?" That was older than her whole school building. "That's why it's all dented. It's not old by accident. It's old because it's actually old." She tested the idea in her head: if the same cup had been handed to a new team every single spring for more than a hundred years, of course it would look worn. The dents weren't carelessness. They were history, the way the old forest trail behind her house looked worn because a whole ecosystem of deer and rabbits and runners had used it forever.

She climbed back to her seat and told Adriana and Colt the whole thing before the second period started. Colt looked at the screen again, at all those carved rings of names stacked below the bowl. "So it's like a family heirloom," he said slowly, "except the family is every team that ever won it."

"Exactly," Megan said. Down on the ice, the home team scored, and the stadium roared so loud her foam finger vibrated in her hand.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Nolan held up two shirts in the clothing store, one with a sailboat printed on it, the little hull stretching across the chest, and one with a flock of migratory geese flying over a lake. He was eleven and had never once cared what his shirt said, but the school dance was on Friday, and apparently that changed everything.

"Get the geese," said Adem, sliding his sunglasses down his nose even though they were indoors. "The geese say mysterious. The boat says you own a canoe." Vienna, who was there purely to find a headband with a star on it, shook her head. "The boat. Boats are calm. Geese chase people." She had been hunting that headband for three weeks and had dragged them to four stores, and she was not leaving without it.

At the checkout, a bin of glow sticks sat beside the register, and Nolan bought a handful, because the gym would be dark except for them. On Friday night, he found out something odd. The stick he'd kept in his warm pocket all afternoon blazed like a tiny green sun, brighter than anyone else's, but by the second slow song it had faded to almost nothing. Vienna, who had kept hers in her jacket pocket near the cold drinks, had a dimmer stick that was still going strong. Nolan turned his dead stick over in his fingers and thought about it. Warm meant bright and short. Cold meant dim and long.

So he ran a test. He cracked his last two sticks, tucked one into his sock near the cold door where the drinks were stacked, and held the other in his fist the whole next fast song. When the lights came up, the warm one in his fist was already pale, and the cold one still glowed, faint but stubborn, like it was refusing to quit.

"Watch this," Nolan said afterward, when Vienna and Adem came over to his house for snacks. He dropped his last living stick, the cold-tested one, into the freezer and shut the door. Adem pressed his face against the frosty white hull of the freezer like a man peering through a porthole. "If cold makes them last," Vienna said slowly, "then the freezer should transform it into the longest glow ever." At breakfast the next morning, they gathered around, and Nolan pulled open the door.

There it was, pale green, still burning, and Adem whispered, "It survived the night."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
Xavier had never done laundry before, and tonight it mattered. His older sister had a job interview at nine the next morning, and she was stuck closing at the diner until eleven, so she had handed him a hamper, two quarters short of a full dollar, and the words "my grey interview shirt is in there somewhere."

The laundromat hummed around him, warm and smelling like soap and hot metal. Mr. Aquino, who ran the place, sat behind the counter fixing a fan with a screwdriver while a portable generator outside rattled backup power to half the machines. Xavier's friends Milan and Hunter had come along mostly to buy snacks from the vending wall, but Milan proved useful, pulling the hamper apart on the folding table. "Dark stuff together," Milan said, "lights together, or the colours bleed." Hunter held up a red sock next to a white towel as evidence. Xavier sorted, thinking his sister had sorted for him for years without him ever noticing. It felt fundamental, like learning how the water got hot in the first place.

He got the wash going and then, while it tumbled, the three of them argued about whether the town should advocate for a later school start time, which ate up forty minutes without anyone conceding anything. When the dryer finally buzzed, Hunter said his mom was picking him up, and Xavier let the load sit. He and Milan played cards on the folding table. The minutes slid by. By the time Xavier pulled the clothes out, the grey shirt was creased all over, sharp lines pressed into the collar and sleeves like it had been slept in.

He hung it up and tugged at the wrinkles, but they stayed. Milan squinted at the shirt, then at the still-warm dryer next to theirs, where another customer's clothes were spinning. "Wait," Milan said. "Remember last month? My hoodie came out fine when I folded it right away, but when I left it overnight it looked like a raisin." Xavier held the wrinkled shirt beside a towel he had pulled out hot and folded immediately, which lay flat and smooth on the table. The difference was obvious. The clothes had cooled crumpled, and cooling crumpled had set the creases.

Xavier ran home, filled the bathroom sink with hot water, and dipped the shirt through it, then hung it straight while it steamed. In the morning his sister found it hanging, nearly smooth, and pressed the last small wrinkles out with her palm. She didn't know about the dryer, or the card game, or the raisin hoodie. She just said, "You actually did it," and Xavier, watching from the hallway, decided not to tell her how close it had been. The front door clicked shut behind her, and he went back to fold the rest of the basket while it was still warm.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A tyre's recommended pressure is printed on its sidewall, often in psi or bar.
story:
The flat tyre lay on the garage floor between Jacob's knees, and Warren stood over him eating the last of the crackers. Jacob had the levers tucked under the tyre's edge, working the second one around the rim. The old tube came out with a soft hiss, and he held it up to the window light until he found the puncture, a pinhole near the valve.

Mr. O'Brien, who owned the garage, had left a new tube and a hand pump on the bench. "You patch it or swap it, your choice," he had said. Jacob swapped it, pushing the new tube inside the tyre and snapping the bead back over the rim with his thumbs. Then came the pumping. He counted the strokes out loud, twenty, thirty, forty, and squeezed the tyre with his hand. It still felt soft, like a loaf of bread that hadn't risen.

"I think it takes about twenty psi," Warren said, still watching. "My dad talks about psi all the time."

Jacob pumped another forty strokes and squeezed again. Barely different. He sat back on the cold concrete and thought. If the tyre looked the same and felt the same after eighty strokes, either the pump was broken or the tyre needed far more than they guessed. He could infer one thing, though: the pump was pushing air, because the hose stiffened on every stroke. So the problem was the target, not the tool.

He tipped the wheel and ran his thumb along the black sidewall, where thin raised letters caught the light. Halfway around he found them, moulded into the rubber: a pressure range, printed right on the tyre, with the numbers given in psi and also in bar. It wanted more than three times Warren's guess.

"That's a lot of pumping," Warren said.

"It's the number printed on the side," Jacob said. "Psi or bar, it says both."

Allie came in from the driveway, where she'd been scraping grey lichen off the wall of the garage with a putty knife because Mr. O'Brien had promised her five dollars for it. She took over the pumping while Jacob counted, and they traded off every hundred strokes. When the gauge on the pump finally climbed into the printed range, Jacob pressed his palm against the tyre. It was hard as a melon.

They wheeled the bike out into the sun and Jacob spun the pedals once with his foot. "Hop on," he said to Warren. "Let's see if it stays up."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
story:
Brielle had guessed the food bank would be quiet, but the sorting room sounded like a gymnasium where everyone whispered. Mr. Lewandowski handed her a clipboard with a list of expired codes. "Your job is to enforce this rule," he said, tapping the dates. "Anything past the cutoff goes in the gray bin."

She started on a crate of peanut butter. Angelica, sorting beside her, held up a dented can. "How long have food banks even existed in Canada?" she asked. "Like, a hundred years? Since pioneers?"

"Obviously forever," said Tatum from the next table. "People have always needed food."

Brielle turned a jar over and thought about it. Last summer she had helped her grandmother clean out a pantry and found a jar of pickles with a faded newspaper label. Her grandmother had laughed and said the store had closed before Brielle was born. Things carried their own history if you looked at the edges. "They haven't always existed," Brielle said slowly. "They had to start somewhere. I bet it was recently, like the eighties. Somewhere big, like Toronto."

"Toronto," Tatum agreed. "Everything starts in Toronto."

"You're both wrong," said a voice behind them. Mr. Lewandowski was reading the question off a poster taped to the wall, one Brielle had walked past three times without noticing. It showed a photo of a small storefront with a hand-painted sign. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta," he read, then added, "not Toronto. Not even close."

"1981?" Angelica said. "That's before my mom finished school."

"So it's younger than my parents' car," Tatum said, "and their car barely runs."

Brielle kept sorting, but her mind snagged on the number. If the first one opened in 1981 in Edmonton, then somewhere in this room there might be proof. She picked up a dusty box from the bottom of the stack, the kind nobody wanted to lift. Inside, under the canned peas, she found a yellowed volunteer manual with a printing date of 1993 and, on the first page, a short history section. Edmonton. 1981. The words matched the poster exactly. She held it up like a trophy. "I tested it," she announced. "The manual agrees with the poster."

"You did a whole investigation over a bet we didn't make," Angelica said.

"I like being right on principle."

Mr. Lewandowski walked over, looked at the manual, and wrote something on his clipboard. "Saturday crew historian," he said. "Resilient worker, too. That box weighed a ton."

"Resilient," Tatum repeated. "Big word for someone who sorts peanut butter."

"I'm also the narrator of this whole afternoon," Brielle said, gesturing at the room, the gray bin, the clipboard. "When people ask how it went, I decide the story."

"Then make me sound taller," Tatum said.

Brielle dropped another jar into the gray bin and marked her list. "No promises."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Asher slid into his seat in the computer lab just as Ms. Sok said, "Open your spreadsheet, and this time make the chart yourself." On the board she had left two columns of numbers: how many books each homeroom had collected for the library drive. Asher's job was to add each column with a formula and turn the totals into a bar chart. He typed =SUM, dragged his cursor down the column for Room 12, and watched the number appear like magic. Room 12 had 143 books. Room 9 had 149.

"Just six apart," said Maeva, leaning over from the next computer. She was still fighting with her own sum, which kept saying 0 because her formula grabbed an empty cell. Asher showed her how to highlight the right boxes, and she grinned and tried again on her own.

Then he made the chart, and his stomach dropped. The bar for Room 9 towered over the bar for Room 12, three times taller, like a giant next to a mouse. Six books out of more than a hundred, and it looked like Room 9 had crushed them. Keon, whose homeroom was Room 9, was already crowing across the lab. "Look at that! We demolished you!"

Asher stared at the chart instead of answering. Something had to be wrong, but he couldn't see what. Both bars started from the same bottom line, didn't they? He followed the little marks up the side of the chart with his finger and stopped. The axis didn't start at zero. It started at 135. Below that, the chart simply wasn't there, so Room 12's bar could only show the tiny part above 135, while Room 9's bar looked enormous. He remembered the seed experiment in science, how you couldn't judge a seed by its hull until you split it open. This chart had a hull too, and he had believed what was on the outside.

He tested it. In the chart settings he changed the minimum value to zero, clicked apply, and both bars leapt upward, nearly the same height. Room 9 was ahead, sure, but only by a sliver. Then he thought of the fundraising posters in the hallway, the ones that made one grade's total look huge, and wondered how many of those charts started above zero too. A chart could diminish his whole class's work without anyone lying out loud.

"Ms. Sok," he called, waving her over. "Look what happens when the axis starts at 135 instead of zero."

Keon came to look too, arms crossed, his smirk fading to something more thoughtful as the bars evened out. "Huh," he said. "Still ahead, though."

"By six," said Asher.

Keon shrugged, but he pulled his chair over to Maeva's screen. "Hey, your formula grabbed an empty box. Want me to show you what he showed me?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
The car smelled like Grandma Ruth's coffee cake, which sat in a tin on Audrey's lap, untouched since the funeral that morning. Dad drove with both hands on the wheel, quiet the whole way back from the cemetery. Audrey kept thinking about the seven days ahead, when people would stream through their house, and she could not figure out what any of them were supposed to say to her. Sorry your grandma died felt clumsy. Nothing felt right. She opened the tin, closed it again, and watched the houses slide past.

"Dad," she said, "what do I say to people when they come tomorrow?"

He was quiet for a moment. "You don't have to say anything. It's called shiva. It means seven, seven days after the burial, when people come to comfort us."

"So they come just to stand there?"

"Just about."

That did not seem like a plan. Audrey liked plans. She decided to test it, the way she tested things in science class. If the visitors were coming only to be present, then the probability that anyone expected a speech from her was low, maybe one in ten. She would run the experiment tomorrow: stay in the room, say almost nothing, and see whether anyone looked disappointed.

By the second day, the living room smelled of coffee and onions, and Audrey's experiment was failing in a strange way. Nobody was disappointed. Martha came after school and sat beside her on the couch for an hour, and the longest sentence either of them managed was about the cafeteria's new pizza. Martha did not seem to mind. She kept coming back, too, every single day, as if the silence were something worth persisting through.

On the fifth day Diya arrived, hesitant in the doorway, holding a grocery bag with both hands. Diya had moved here in September and had never been to anything like this. She walked over and set the bag on the coffee table. Inside were three boxes of the exact coffee cake Grandma Ruth used to bake, the kind with the swirl through the middle.

"I didn't know what you were supposed to bring," Diya said. "So I brought cake. Is that wrong?"

Audrey looked at the boxes, then at Diya's worried face, and something in her chest loosened for the first time all week. Her experiment had been set up wrong from the start. It was never about testing what she should say. It was about finding out what everyone else was doing, and now she knew: nothing, and everything, just showing up, day after day, until the seven days were done.

"It's the opposite of wrong," Audrey said, and cut them both a slice.
